subject: psychology
topicDisplay: Options: Abnormal, Developmental, Health & Human Relationships
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Abnormal psychology (diagnosis, aetiology and treatment of disorders)
Health psychology (determinants, health problems and promotion)
Developmental psychology (influences on development, cognitive and social development)
Psychology of human relationships (personal, group and social responsibility)

questions.q: The two major classification systems used to diagnose mental disorders are the DSM-5 and the:
questions.explain: Clinicians use the DSM-5 and the World Health Organization's ICD to classify and diagnose mental disorders.

questions.q: Rosenhan's 'On being sane in insane places' is often used to question the:
options: Validity and reliability of psychiatric diagnosis
questions.explain: Pseudopatients were admitted and labelled despite behaving normally, raising doubts about diagnostic validity and reliability.

questions.q: Beck's cognitive model of depression centres on the negative cognitive triad: negative views of the self, the world and the:
questions.explain: Beck argued that depression involves automatic negative thoughts about oneself, the world and the future.

questions.q: Seligman's concept of learned helplessness explains depression as arising from:
options: A perceived lack of control over aversive events
questions.explain: Repeated exposure to uncontrollable negative events can produce a helpless, passive state linked to depression.

questions.q: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) treat depression by increasing the availability of:
questions.explain: SSRIs block reuptake of serotonin at the synapse, increasing its availability, though effectiveness varies between individuals.

questions.q: A clinician notes that the same cluster of symptoms is interpreted and labelled differently across cultures. This is a problem of:
options: Cultural considerations in the validity of diagnosis
questions.explain: Cultural variation in how distress is expressed and interpreted challenges the cross-cultural validity of diagnostic categories.

questions.q: Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome describes three stages of the stress response: alarm, resistance and:
questions.explain: Prolonged stress moves from alarm through resistance to exhaustion, when the body's resources are depleted.

questions.q: The biopsychosocial model of health proposes that health and illness are determined by:
options: Biological, psychological and social factors interacting
questions.explain: The model integrates physiological, cognitive-emotional and social influences rather than reducing health to biology alone.

questions.q: A 'risk factor' for a health problem is a variable that:
options: Increases the likelihood of developing the problem
Has no relationship to the problem
questions.explain: Risk factors raise probability but are not deterministic; protective factors lower it.

questions.q: Fear appeals in health promotion are most likely to fail when they:
options: Arouse high fear without giving people a clear, achievable way to respond
questions.explain: Fear appeals work best when combined with efficacy information; fear alone can trigger denial or avoidance.

questions.q: A stop-smoking campaign presents a health threat and also gives specific, manageable steps to quit. This design is likely to be effective because it:
options: Combines a threat with response and self-efficacy information
questions.explain: Pairing threat with clear, achievable actions supports behaviour change, consistent with health-promotion research.

questions.q: Prochaska's stages-of-change model runs precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and:
questions.explain: The transtheoretical model ends with maintenance, sustaining the new behaviour and avoiding relapse.

questions.q: Ainsworth's 'Strange Situation' procedure was designed to assess:
options: The quality or type of infant attachment
questions.explain: The structured observation classifies attachment as secure, insecure-avoidant or insecure-resistant based on the infant's behaviour.

questions.q: Bowlby's attachment theory proposes that early attachment relationships provide:
options: An internal working model that shapes later relationships
questions.explain: The internal working model is a mental template of relationships formed from early attachment that influences later social bonds.

questions.q: In Piaget's theory, object permanence typically develops during the:
questions.explain: Object permanence, understanding that objects continue to exist when out of sight, develops in the sensorimotor stage of infancy.

questions.q: Vygotsky's zone of proximal development refers to the gap between what a child can do:
options: Alone and what they can do with guidance from a more knowledgeable other
In the morning and the afternoon
questions.explain: Learning occurs in the ZPD, where tasks are too hard alone but achievable with appropriate support.

questions.q: Scaffolding in cognitive development involves:
options: Adjusting support to the child's level and reducing it as competence grows
Preventing the child from ever attempting tasks
questions.explain: A more knowledgeable other provides tailored support within the ZPD and withdraws it as the child becomes able to work independently.

questions.q: A teacher gives just enough hints for a pupil to solve a problem slightly beyond their independent ability, then withdraws help as the pupil improves. This best illustrates:
options: Working within the zone of proximal development through scaffolding
questions.explain: Guided support for a task just beyond the pupil's solo ability, gradually withdrawn, is scaffolding within the ZPD.

questions.q: Factors shown to increase interpersonal attraction include proximity, similarity and:
questions.explain: Research links attraction to proximity, similarity and physical attractiveness, among other factors.

questions.q: Sherif's Robbers Cave study supports realistic conflict theory by showing that intergroup hostility arose from:
options: Competition between groups for scarce resources
A lack of any group identity
questions.explain: Introducing competitive, zero-sum tasks between the two boys' groups generated prejudice and conflict.

questions.q: In the Robbers Cave study, Sherif reduced intergroup conflict most effectively by introducing:
questions.explain: Shared goals that neither group could achieve alone required cooperation and reduced hostility.

questions.q: Latane and Darley explained the bystander effect partly through:
questions.explain: When others are present, each individual feels less personal responsibility to intervene, reducing helping.

questions.q: A person witnessing an emergency in a large crowd does not help, assuming someone else will act. This best illustrates:
questions.explain: The presence of many potential helpers spreads responsibility, making any one person less likely to act.

questions.q: Research suggests prosocial behaviour can be encouraged by:
options: Increasing personal responsibility, empathy and positive modelling
questions.explain: Making responsibility explicit, fostering empathy and providing prosocial models all promote helping behaviour.
